transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been troubling you that brought you here today?

Yeah… um, what’s been troubling me is my eating at night, mostly. It’s gotten to where most nights, after my wife goes to bed, I’m still up and I end up in the kitchen, and I don’t just have a snack or a normal plate of food. It’s like I’ll start with leftovers, and then it turns into fried chicken, mac and cheese, sweet potatoes, rolls—whatever’s in there from an event or dinner—and I just keep going.

I mean, it’s not like I’m making a plate and sitting down for a meal. It’s way past that. Sometimes it feels like I look up and a whole tray is gone, or half the fridge is cleaned out. And then I’m standing there realizing how much I ate, and it’s… embarrassing to even say out loud, but that’s really why I’m here. It’s been happening a lot, and it feels like more than I can manage on my own.
Can you describe what goes through your mind while you're eating like this at night? Do you feel like you can stop if you wanted to, or does it feel like you're not in control?

Yeah… it feels like I’m not in control. That’s probably the part that scares me the most, honestly, because before it starts I can have all these thoughts like, “Okay, just don’t go in the kitchen,” or “If you eat something, just have a little bit and go to bed.” But once I take that first bite, it’s like the decision has already been made somewhere else, not by me.

I’ll be standing there eating and, in my head, I’m actually telling myself to stop. Like, I’ll literally think, “George, stop now. Put it away. You’re going to feel awful.” And I know that. I’m aware of it while it’s happening. But my hands just keep moving, like I’m fixing another plate, or opening another container, or going back to see what else is there. It doesn’t feel like I’m calmly choosing it each time. It feels more like I’m watching myself keep going.

And then sometimes I’ll try to bargain with myself, like, “This is the last plate,” or “Just finish this and then you’re done,” but then that line moves. There’s always one more thing. So yeah… if I’m being honest, wanting to stop and actually stopping feel like two completely different things in that moment.
Do these episodes usually happen after you’ve already gone to bed and maybe even fallen asleep, like you wake up and then go to the kitchen to eat?

Um… I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because I don’t think of it as me being fully asleep and then waking up to eat, if that’s what you mean. Most of the time I’m already still up. Like, I haven’t really gone to bed yet, or I’m kind of dragging out the night after my wife has gone to sleep.

I guess there might be times where I’m tired enough that it feels foggy, like I’m half-zoned out, but I wouldn’t say I’m waking up surprised in the kitchen or anything like that. It’s more like I’m awake, I know what I’m doing, and I still end up going in there anyway.
When you're in the kitchen eating like this, do you ever feel like you're on autopilot or not fully aware of what you're doing, like you're in a trance or not completely awake?

I don’t know if I’d call it a trance, exactly. I mean… I’m aware enough to know I’m in the kitchen, I know I’m eating, I know I probably shouldn’t be doing it like that. It’s not like I come to and suddenly realize, “How did I get here?” or anything that extreme.

But it can feel kind of automatic, if that makes sense. Like I’m not thinking each step through the way I would if I were making a normal meal. I’ll just be opening containers, heating things up, standing at the counter, going back for more, and there’s this part of me that’s watching it happen and thinking, “Why are you doing this?” But I still keep doing it.

So… not asleep, not totally unaware. More like I’m aware but not really steering the car, I guess. I don’t know if that’s what you mean by autopilot.
Do you feel distressed about these nighttime eating episodes, or have they caused problems for you in your daily life, like with your health, relationships, or how you feel about yourself?

Yeah. I mean… yes, absolutely. It bothers me a lot. It’s not just like, “Oh, I ate too much, whatever.” Afterward I feel… honestly, I feel sick with myself. Like there’s this heavy disgust that settles in once it’s over and I’m looking at what I ate or what’s left out, and I just think, “How did I let this happen again?”

And the shame part is probably the worst. Because during the day, I think people see me as someone who has it together — or at least I try really hard to be that person. Organized, reliable, strong, the guy who can handle things. And then at night I’m sitting there in the kitchen or on the couch feeling like I’m hiding this completely different version of myself. It makes me feel guilty and embarrassed, like I’m failing at something basic that everyone else can just control.

It definitely affects how I feel about myself. I wake up the next day already kind of carrying it, like I’ve disappointed myself before the day even starts. And I’ll tell myself I’m going to be different that night, but then if it happens again, the shame just stacks up. It’s hard not to feel disgusted with myself, even though another part of me knows beating myself up doesn’t really help.
Have you ever gotten up during the night after being asleep and eaten without remembering it the next morning?

No… not that I can think of. I mean, I don’t want to say it’s impossible in some absolute way, because I’m asleep, so how would I know, right? But I haven’t had that thing where I wake up in the morning and find food wrappers or dishes and have no memory of eating.

When it happens, I usually remember it. Sometimes I wish I didn’t, honestly, but I do. I remember going to the kitchen, I remember eating, I remember afterward. It might feel foggy or kind of compulsive in the moment, especially if it’s late and I’m exhausted, but it’s not like I’m blacking out or sleepwalking and then discovering it the next day. So… no, I don’t think I’ve eaten in the night without remembering it.

Have you ever had episodes where you feel like you're eating a very large amount of food in a short period of time, like a discrete period of time—say within a couple of hours—and during that time you feel like you can't stop eating or control how much you're eating?

Yes. Yeah, that’s… that’s exactly what it feels like, actually. It’s not just eating more than I meant to. It’s like once I take that first bite, something switches over, and the decision feels like it’s already been made for me.

I’ll be standing there telling myself, like, “George, stop now. Put it away. You don’t need any more.” And I mean it — I’m not just casually thinking it. I’m really trying to tell myself to stop. But my hands are still moving. I’m fixing another plate, or opening another container, or going back to something I already put away. It’s like there’s this split between what I’m saying in my head and what my body is doing.

And yes, it can be a lot in a short time. Not like a normal second helping where you’re still deciding if you’re hungry. It feels rushed and driven, like I have to keep going until something in me is… I don’t know, shut off or satisfied or just too full to continue. Even while it’s happening I know I’ve passed the point where I wanted to stop, but stopping feels almost impossible in that moment.
Do these episodes where you feel like you can’t control your eating only happen at night, or do they also occur during the day?

I’m not sure I can cleanly separate it by time of day, if that makes sense. The part I’m most aware of is the loss of control itself — like once I take that first bite, it feels like the decision has already been made for me somehow.

I’ll be telling myself, “George, stop now, you don’t have to keep going,” and I really mean it. But then my hands are still moving, like I’m fixing another plate or opening another container before I’ve even fully decided to. That’s the part that scares me, honestly — it feels like I’m watching myself continue even while I’m trying to stop.

So I don’t know if I can give you a neat answer like “only at night” versus “also during the day” without thinking more about it. But the episodes where I feel that out-of-control feeling, that’s what they’re like.
Do you find that these episodes affect your mood, energy, or ability to function during the day, like at work or with your family?

Yeah… it does. I think more than I like to admit, honestly.

It’s not just that I feel bad afterward and then move on. It kind of carries into the next day, or even into how I show up around people. I’ve pulled back from things I used to be pretty involved in — community planning meetings, helping organize events, that kind of stuff. I used to be someone people could count on for that. I liked being useful, you know? Having a role.

But lately I find myself making excuses or just not volunteering in the first place, because I feel embarrassed and drained. I worry people can tell I’m not really holding things together the way I used to. Even if nobody says anything, I’m sitting there thinking they can see it on me somehow — like my energy is off, or I’m distracted, or I just don’t seem like myself.

And then the more I avoid those things, the worse I feel, because it’s like I’m disappearing from parts of my life I actually cared about. So yes, it affects my functioning. Maybe not always in some dramatic way from the outside, but it’s definitely changed what I participate in and how much I let people see me.

Do you feel that these nighttime eating episodes have significantly interfered with your ability to function in important areas of your life, such as work, social activities, or family responsibilities?

Yes, it has. I mean, I don’t want to make it sound like I’m completely unable to do anything, but it has definitely changed how I function, especially socially and with responsibilities I used to take seriously.

I’ve pulled back from community planning meetings and helping with events, which used to be a big part of how I stayed connected. I was the kind of person who would show up, help set things up, make calls, organize little details — not because I had to, but because I liked being useful. And now I find myself avoiding it. I’ll think about going, and then I just feel this wave of embarrassment and exhaustion, like I don’t have the energy to be seen or to pretend I’m doing fine.

Part of it is that I’m afraid people will notice I’m not holding things together the way I used to. Maybe they wouldn’t even notice, but in my head it feels obvious, like I’m carrying it around on me. So I stay away, or I don’t volunteer, or I tell myself someone else can handle it this time.

And then that becomes its own problem, because I feel worse for not showing up. So yes — it’s interfered. Maybe quietly, but significantly.
